summary:
Top Traders Unplugged Systematic Investor 348 (May 2025): Andrew Beer and Niels on why trend following suffered its worst period in years, policy-driven whipsaws and short-term models, and how allocators should judge managers and fees.
Conclusions: sentiment head fakes hurt short-term and innovation-heavy managers; medium-long trend has worked for 50 years; expect a 3% allocation and rebound after drawdowns.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: completely unrealistic that you can move pretty much any of the Apple production back to the US or any other country for that matter
claims.claim: Apple built its supply chain in China (about $275bn pledged 2016-2021, engineers trained locally), so tariff-driven reshoring of production is unrealistic over the near term, which makes trade-war policy hard to trade on fundamentals.
claims.testable: no - industry anecdote from a book

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: around 20 2007 they simply started to uh redeem from all these external trend followers and built the whole capacity internally
claims.claim: A large sovereign wealth fund that hosted staff at trend followers redeemed from them around 2007 and built the capacity internally, an example of institutions internalizing trend following (also via QIS swaps).

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own trend barometer finished yesterday at 25. That's exceptionally weak.
claims.claim: Niels's Trend Barometer at 25 in May 2025 is exceptionally weak, signalling a hostile environment for trend following.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Stocken trend down about uh 3% down 12% for the year
claims.claim: In May 2025 SG Trend was down about 3% (down 12% YTD), SG CTA down 8.69% YTD and BTOP50 down 5.25%, while short-term traders were roughly flat and equities were up 3-6% in May.
claims.indicator: SG Trend, SG CTA, BTOP50, SG Short-Term index, MSCI World, S&P 500

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: very very few markets that have given any kind of trends that can be traded
claims.claim: In 2025 up to May very few markets gave tradable trends; many reversed once or twice, and losses came mainly from fixed income and precious metals giving back gains.
claims.indicator: number of trending markets, fixed income and precious metals P&L

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: one of the problems for allocators right now is it's very hard to distinguish the signal when sometimes the policy is about noise
claims.claim: Policy announcements such as Liberation Day tariffs were chosen without analysis, so policy signals are noisy and macro views built on them are hard to trade.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: unlike other areas of the business world that we're used to, the negotiation is often the point
claims.claim: Trump's policy style treats negotiation as the goal with no need for consistency or do-no-harm, so announcements reverse and create whipsaws in markets.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: And the problem with short-term models is they're really gullible, right?
claims.claim: Short-term trend models take news-driven moves (e.g. a tweet) at face value, so they get whipsawed in headline-driven markets, whereas long-term models wait for confirmation.
claims.testable: yes - compare lookbacks in reversal regimes

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: since the peak in 2022, we've had five vicious reversals, right?
claims.claim: Since the 2022 peak there were five vicious reversals (inflation not falling, SVB, Powell pivot, growth fear plus yen carry unwind, Liberation Day), which created repeated drawdowns for trend followers.
claims.testable: yes - reversal counts and CTA drawdowns

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you get head faked out two or three times on on on the way. So it's kind of a zero sharp ratio strategy over time
claims.claim: Short-term models enter trends early but get head-faked two or three times on the way, giving roughly zero Sharpe over time; they may hurt in policy-noise regimes like the 2016-2020 Long Winter.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: going back to what's really worked for 50 years which is is is is the medium to long-term trend models
claims.claim: Medium to long-term trend models are the core that has worked for 50 years and may outperform the innovations (short-term models, vol controls, alt markets) added to protect against whipsaws.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the worst time frame is actually the 130 days
claims.claim: In Niels's YTD 2025 test varying only lookback, the 20-day outperformed 60-day, which outperformed 260-day, and the 130-day was worst, so medium-term was not the safe haven.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a lot of people gravitated towards the medium-term because of size, right?
claims.claim: Many CTAs favour medium-term models because of capacity, and some managers believe medium term is uniquely best.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: not actually through speed of models but it could be through different ways of looking at risk management for example
claims.claim: Rather than speeding up models, whipsaw protection may come from improved risk management.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the asen index is down 15% year-over-year um through the end of April that matches or slightly exceeds its largest historical draw down going back to 2000
claims.claim: The SG trend/CTA index was down 15% year over year to April 2025, matching its worst drawdown since 2000, and managers built on shorter models, vol controls, active position management and alternative markets had drawdowns worse than the space.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: individual managers who um uh you know who had basically built their thesis around better risk management and risk controls
claims.claim: Managers whose pitch was better risk controls and innovation (short models, vol controls, position management, alternative markets) suffered worse drawdowns than plain trend, suggesting those features failed in this environment.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: at some point you have strong central banks and weak politicians and then at some point you have strong politicians and weak central banks
claims.claim: A cycle exists between strong central banks with weak politicians and the reverse; after a period of Fed control, 2025 resembles strong politicians and weak central banks, where Trump rather than Powell moves markets.
claims.indicator: central bank vs political dominance regime

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I have also observed that even managers who've been around for a long time, two, three, four decades, some of them are hitting their worst draw downs uh ever right now
claims.claim: Even managers with 20-40 year histories were hitting their worst drawdowns in 2025, consistent with longevity eventually producing a worst period.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I feel absolutely certain that we're going to go back and we're going to make new highs
claims.claim: Niels expects trend following to make new highs again as models adjust and markets begin trending, with investor emotional reactions the main concern.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: people will at some point probably soon declare trend following dead once again and it's usually the best time to to buy or add uh to it
claims.claim: Trend following is declared dead after drawdowns, and that is usually the best time to buy or add.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the whole point of managed futures is you sell your losers right you don't hold on to them you don't double down
claims.claim: Unlike value investing (Buffett holding through 50% drawdowns), managed futures has no intrinsic-value anchor and cuts losers, so one cannot argue that cheaper means rebound; communication must rely on the information story.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: The information is going to change between now and when you next measure it and the sentiment about that information is going to change as well.
claims.claim: Price moves have two components, changing information and changing sentiment, which compete; managed futures profit when they detect true changes in information.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the space was on fire in the beginning of 2024. Why? Because it picked up on the Trump trade early
claims.claim: In early 2024 CTAs picked up the post-election information shift early (long equities, dollar, gold, rate cuts priced out) before sentiment whipsaws began after April.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we went short treasuries in September of 2020. Think about how early that was
claims.claim: Trend picks up changes in information early: short Treasuries in September 2020 when yields rose from 0.50% to 0.70%, a contrarian move signalling inflation before consensus.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: there are all these kind of sentiment head fakes
claims.claim: Since April 2024 information changed little but sentiment head fakes caused a 15% SG CTA drawdown in a series of 2-5% drops without time to recover, like the 2022-2023 drawdown.
claims.conditions: sentiment flips without lasting information change

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the bet that you have to make on the space is that the world is actually going to change and the change in information is going to drown out the change in in in sentiment
claims.claim: Trend following works if real information changes eventually outweigh sentiment noise.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: inflation's going to go the dollar is going to people are going to lose confidence in the dollar
claims.claim: Andrew expects big things to break (inflation up, confidence in the dollar lost) as policy risk-taking spirals, creating the money-making opportunity for managed futures.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: bonds have essentially had something like five reversals in the last 12 months or so, which is a lot
claims.claim: Bonds had about five reversals in 12 months, equities a couple, and dollar and energies also reversed, tricking managers into flipping exposure (a perfect storm).
claims.indicator: number of trend reversals by asset

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: what is the max draw down in relation to its annualized volatility and people will be surprised I think that
claims.claim: Measured as max drawdown relative to annualised volatility over 12 years, bonds have by far the worst ratio and equities are not better than many CTA managers, so current CTA drawdowns are not extreme in relative terms.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: oh these alternative markets they trend better
claims.claim: The alternative-markets-trend-better narrative worked for a couple of years then failed for three to four years, partly because momentum disappeared as people crowded into them.
claims.testable: yes - alt vs core markets trend Sharpe over time

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I think the core driver the core beta of managed futures was discovered 50 years ago.
claims.claim: The core trend beta was discovered decades ago; when banks offered QIS products and GSA a 50bp product in the early 2010s it was commoditised, pushing managers to differentiate through added features.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the narrative followed positioning luck because then after the money comes in, they have not
claims.claim: A trend fund with luckily positioned March 2020 and strong 2020-2021 grew to $5bn; narrative reinforced skill, assets flowed in, then it lagged, a recurring flow-chasing pattern.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: people that I think are very very smart and and respect have looked at that issue and have not found evidence of it
claims.claim: Smart researchers found no evidence that alternative markets trend more; they mainly provide diversification.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: Go back 3 years ago. Show me the model you had then and how it would have done and and have these things that you've done.
claims.claim: Allocators should ask managers to backtest their announced enhancements (more markets, vol controls, short-term models) against the model of 3 and 6 years ago to see if complexity adds value.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: underperformed the other 19 guys in the stock CTA index by by by by 20%
claims.claim: Model overhauls can go either way: AQR rebuilt its models and is doing very well but from 2014 to 2020 underperformed the other 19 SG CTA constituents by 20%.
claims.indicator: AQR relative performance to SG CTA constituents

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think it's fair to judge pe judge firms which which we all get judged from from the performance from the relative performance
claims.claim: Managers should be judged on relative performance rather than asked to justify individual model changes, since changes are made believing they are better and hypothetical comparisons are impractical.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the bonus is on the manager to to to explain why they why somebody should be be paying 170 basis points, not 85 basis points
claims.claim: With cheap replication and bank trend products available as benchmarks, managers must justify higher fees relative to such alternatives.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we can outperform three to 400 basis points to the index and then 5 years later you look at the numbers and they outperformed by 50 basis points
claims.claim: Replicators also over-promise: a 300-400bp outperformance claim ended as about 50bp after five years.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we were slow with SVB. We were slow with the second Powell pivot
claims.claim: The weekly replicator underperformed in 2023 because it was slow at SVB and the second Powell pivot; its track record still met promised numbers since 2016, and outcomes depend on the window used.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: what should be your expectation of to how much value they would add to warrant an additional 100 basis points? To me, it's three or 400 basis points
claims.claim: Each additional 100bp of fees should require 300-400bp of added value because added complexity also raises trading costs.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: our trading costs on in in in US land are eight basis points or something like that because we're just trading these 10 super liquid contracts
claims.claim: Trading only 10 super-liquid contracts gives about 8bp of trading costs, whereas a competitor trading many more markets shows about 200bp, so complex programs must beat cheap ones by a wide margin.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: suddenly they had their worst draw down by some margin was actually 2012 12 or 2013
claims.claim: Long-established managers had their worst drawdowns in 2012-2013 in an under-the-radar period, followed by about five flat years and then among the best-ever years, suggesting drawdowns precede strong periods.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it just keeps coming back to this 4 and a half% and we're a little bit above that
claims.claim: The 10-year yield keeps returning to about 4.5% despite attempts to push it lower, and Niels suspects interest rates could be where markets break.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they are slow on purpose and and they have told they have told their end investors that you should not panic and you should not move fast
claims.claim: Managed futures alpha is not zero-sum between managers but earned against slow-moving 60/40 investors who are slow by design and constrained by their justification (e.g. inflation never returning), so even convinced allocators cannot change quickly.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you can get that in the 10-year Treasury you don't need that in 32 different different um uh instruments
claims.claim: Replication works because it captures managed futures trading against slow investors using a few instruments such as the 10-year Treasury; niche markets like palm oil add little for that edge.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you can great outsized gains by having static position size, but you can have great outsized losses by having static position size as we're seeing now
claims.claim: Managers with few markets, bigger risk in smaller markets and static position sizing had top returns over five years but outsized losses now.
claims.indicator: static vs dynamic position sizing, concentration

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they're now obviously not able to keep up because the alpha is hurting, but the beta is back to where it was
claims.claim: Return-stacked managed futures plus equity products lag now that CTA alpha is negative and equity beta has recovered, behaving exactly as designed.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: if history is anything to go by the best time to buy this strategy is in the draw down
claims.claim: Historically the best time to buy trend following has been in drawdowns because strategies subsequently made new highs.
claims.indicator: CTA drawdown depth then forward return

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: bonds have failed miserably right since since the end of 2000 I mean including this year by the way
claims.claim: Bonds have failed since 2020 (inflation not transitory, high stock-bond correlation), which will drive trend into wealth-management portfolios; allocators avoid admitting the mistake of holding 40% in bonds.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: people will fire managers who have done who have underperformed their expectations
claims.claim: After underperformance expect musical chairs: managers fired, some investors leave the space, and money flows to recent winners (AQR, Campbell, a CTA ETF), as in the late 2010s.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they're not 90% correlated to the CTA index, 80% correlated with with like a little bit of enhancements here or there
claims.claim: Recent winners are not highly correlated to the CTA index (not 90%) and differ materially, while others will seek cheaper beta-like exposure that suits replication.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: April called into question whether you could rely on manage futures in a sharp inflection point
claims.claim: April 2025's performance weakened demand for stacked managed futures plus equity products (e.g. a UCITS fund with a $200m weekly outflow), delaying adoption.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it needs to be big enough that in 2022, the next time there's a 2022, you can point to it and say, "Look, we've got this beacon of green and a sea of red."
claims.claim: Managed futures should be about a 3% allocation: large enough to matter in a 2022-type event but small enough to hide in the tall grass in years like 2025.
claims.testable: yes - portfolio optimisation with behavioural constraint

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: when you move into the wealth management space, the language needs to change
claims.claim: Selling trend to wealth managers requires a narrative that fits their constructs, not statistical obviousness aimed at institutional allocators.
